rows.grounds: text in which the teaching is given
description of the Kula secret text

items.question: Who spoke this teaching and in which text was it revealed?
premises: The Blessed Lord himself spoke the teaching.
He spoke it in the glorious Kula secret text.
That text bears true names grounded in the unity of power and its holder.
items.inference: The doctrine of the poison-principle is transmitted by the Lord in the Kula scripture where names reflect the unity of Śakti and Śaktimat.
uncertainties: The exact title or identity of the 'śrīmatkulaguhkara' text is not specified in this verse.
items.plain_english: The Blessed Lord himself spoke this in the glorious Kula secret, a text whose names are truly meaningful because they arise from the unity of Power and the Possessor of Power.

rows.grounds: form of the practice or state
name and nature of the revealed principle

items.question: What is the poison-principle called anacka and how was it revealed?
premises: The poison-principle called anacka has the form of a crow's beak cavity.
It is free from meditation and concentration.
It was revealed out of affection to the listener.
items.inference: Anacka, the poison-principle, is a direct, technique-free realization disclosed by the Lord out of love.
uncertainties: The precise yogic or phonetic referent of 'crow's beak cavity' is not fully explained here.
items.plain_english: Out of affection for you, the Lord revealed the poison-principle called anacka, which has the shape of a crow's beak cavity and is free from meditation and concentration.

items.question: How are the principles of desire and poison understood in their true nature?
premises: The principle of desire is fullness, clearly perceived in the collision of energies.
The principle of poison is nectar.
Poison becomes nectar when the covering of the limited self has fallen away.
items.inference: Desire and poison reveal their highest nature as fullness and nectar when experienced without the contraction of the limited self.
uncertainties: The exact referent of 'saṃghaṭṭa' (collision) may be sexual, energetic, or cognitive depending on context.
items.plain_english: The true nature of desire is fullness, clearly seen in the moment of collision; and the true nature of poison is nectar, once the covering of the limited self has dropped away.

rows.grounds: reason poison is associated with covering
manifest aspect of the same reality

items.question: Why is the pervading power called poison and how does it relate to the supreme abode?
premises: The pervading power is called poison because it can cover the light of the unpervading limited being.
The supreme abode is stainless and beyond taint.
Yet the principle of that same abode also appears with a tinge in manifestation.
items.inference: Poison names the pervading power insofar as it veils the limited self, while the same reality is stainless in its supreme state and tinged in manifestation.
uncertainties: The syntax of 'avyāptuśchādayenmahaḥ' is compressed and allows slight interpretive variation.
items.plain_english: The pervading power is called poison because it can cover the light of the unpervading, limited being; the supreme abode is stainless, yet its principle also appears with a tinge.

rows.grounds: equivalent of will in this context
quality of the goddess/action in essence

items.question: How do will, knowledge, and action map onto desire, poison, and the goddess?
premises: The universe, whose nature is the power of action, flashes forth from that reality.
Will is identified with desire.
Knowledge is identified with poison, and action is the stainless goddess.
items.inference: The triad of will, knowledge, and action appears as desire, poison, and the stainless goddess, through which the universe manifests.
uncertainties: The neuter 'nirañjanam' agrees loosely with 'devī' in this compressed doctrinal mapping.
items.plain_english: Because the universe, made of the power of action, flashes forth from that reality, will is desire, knowledge is poison, and action is the stainless goddess.

rows.grounds: unified absorption in will, knowledge, and action

items.question: What is the realization of the triad and what instruction did the teachers give about it?
premises: Immersion in the triad of will, knowledge, and action is called Śiva or Bhairava.
The teachers instructed that one should become firmly established in this.
This establishment should be maintained always.
items.inference: The supreme state is the lived immersion in the triad, and the gurus enjoin constant establishment in that state.
items.plain_english: Immersion in this triad is called Śiva, Bhairava. Our teachers told us that one should always become firmly established in it.

items.question: How should one contemplate after entering the poison-principle?
premises: Having fully entered the poison-principle, one negates element, poison, and seizing force.
The contemplation affirms 'I alone am'.
Through this contemplation one shines forth.
items.inference: Entry into the poison-principle culminates in a nondual awareness where only the pure 'I' shines.
uncertainties: 'Graha' can mean a seizing entity, planet, or affliction; the exact nuance is context-dependent.
items.plain_english: Having fully entered the poison-principle, one should shine forth with the contemplation: not an element, not poison, and not a seizing force—only 'I alone am.'

items.question: If birth is said to arise from the ṣaṇṭha phonemes, how can ṣaṇṭha-ness apply here?
premises: An objection states that birth is said to arise from the ṣaṇṭha phonemes.
This would seem to imply ṣaṇṭha-ness in the present context.
The reply denies that the ṣaṇṭha is the progenitor here.
items.inference: The term ṣaṇṭha is used in a special sense here, not as the literal source of birth.
uncertainties: The technical phonetic group referred to as 'ṣaṇṭha' depends on the Tantric phoneme classification assumed by the text.
items.plain_english: An objection arises: if birth is said to come from the ṣaṇṭha phonemes, how can there be ṣaṇṭha-ness here? We reply: in this case, the ṣaṇṭha is not the progenitor.

rows.grounds: locates the power in that context

items.question: What power is responsible for bringing forth manifestation in this context?
premises: The power present there is called the power of will.
That very power brings forth its own task.
It brings it forth from within, in the form of its own desired object.
items.inference: Will-power alone is the inner creative agent that manifests its intended form.
items.plain_english: For the power present there, which is called the power of will, itself brings forth its own inner task in the form of what it desires.

items.question: What produces turbidity and the tainted form in manifestation?
premises: A sought-after factor that causes tainting is present in that context.
The birth in question arises from that, not merely from a part.
From that arises turbidity and its corresponding form.
items.inference: Impurity in manifestation comes from a tainting cause within the process, not from the pure creative power alone.
uncertainties: The precise referent of 'eṣitavya' (the thing sought) is doctrinally compressed.
items.plain_english: But where a sought-after cause of tainting is present, the birth that arises from that—not from a mere part—produces turbidity and the form that belongs to it.

items.question: Why is the aggregate called ṣaṇṭha in this teaching?
premises: The aggregate is joined with the tainting of the knowable.
It lacks both the nature of an agitator and the nature of a ground of agitation.
Because of this, the wise call it ṣaṇṭha.
items.inference: Ṣaṇṭha names a tainted aggregate that neither actively agitates nor serves as the true ground of agitation.
uncertainties: The technical sense of 'kṣobha-dhāmatva' is specific to this phonemic-cosmological analysis.
items.plain_english: The wise know that aggregate, joined with the tainting of the knowable, as ṣaṇṭha, because it lacks both the power to agitate and the nature of being the ground of agitation.

items.question: Why was this group of four phonemes named ūṣma by Bhairava?
premises: There is a group of four phonemes under discussion.
It shines with its own heat.
Bhairava of pure nature declared its name to be ūṣma.
items.inference: The phoneme group is called ūṣma because its defining quality is self-generated heat or fervor.
items.plain_english: Bhairava of pure nature declared that this group of four phonemes is called ūṣma, because it shines with its own heat.

items.question: What role do the phonemes from ka to ha play in the process of agitation?
premises: The wise declare the range from ka to ha to be the support of agitation.
When it is joined in the form of the womb, a further agitation arises.
Thus phonemic structure participates in creative stirring.
items.inference: The ka-to-ha range functions as the ground of agitation, and its union with the womb-principle generates further creative movement.
uncertainties: The exact referent of 'yoni-rūpa' here may be phonetic, energetic, or cosmological.
items.plain_english: The wise say that the phonemes from ka to ha are the support of agitation; when that too is joined in the form of the womb, it moves into a further agitation.

items.question: How does the fiftieth phoneme arise and where is it established?
premises: By connection with the indication of that process, the fiftieth phoneme comes into view.
It is well established in the level known as the twenty-fifth.
This establishment follows the pattern described earlier.
items.inference: The fiftieth phoneme is derived through this process and grounded in the twenty-fifth level of the system.
uncertainties: The verse is highly compressed and depends on the preceding phonemic mapping for full clarity.
items.plain_english: Through that indication, the fiftieth phoneme arises, well established as before in the level known as the twenty-fifth.

items.question: How are the two tetrads characterized in relation to difference and non-difference?
premises: There are two tetrads arranged in sequence.
They operate in the mode of difference and non-difference.
The first tetrad is skilled in joining the divisions of consciousness.
items.inference: The phonemic tetrads articulate the play of difference and unity, with the first tetrad reintegrating divided consciousness.
items.plain_english: There are two tetrads, in sequence, moving in difference and non-difference; the first tetrad is skilled in joining together the divisions of consciousness.

items.question: What is the function of the second tetrad and what is the primordial nature of all phonemes?
premises: The other tetrad is the single cause for establishing difference within non-difference.
All collections of phonemes are included in this account.
Originally, all phonemes are made of vowels.
items.inference: The phonemic system unfolds difference within unity, and its primordial substance is vowel-nature.
items.plain_english: The other tetrad is the sole cause by which difference becomes established within non-difference; thus, whatever collection of phonemes there is, all of it was originally made of vowels.

items.question: How do consonants depend on vowels and what is the root of the phoneme stream?
premises: A consonant arises through connection with manifestation.
Consonants have vowels as their life-breath.
In the stream of phonemes, the root is only the group of six vowels.
items.inference: Consonants are dependent manifestations, while a sixfold set of vowels is the living root of all phonemic emanation.
uncertainties: The identity of the 'six' vowels follows a specific Tantric phonemic scheme not fully spelled out here.
items.plain_english: A consonant becomes manifest through articulation, but its life-breath is the vowel; indeed, in the whole stream of phonemes, the root is only the group of six vowels.

rows.grounds: divine correlates of the six vowels

items.question: How are the six vowels correlated with solar and lunar principles?
premises: The six deities are identified with the principal rays of the sun.
Within those solar rays there is a lunar digit.
This inner lunar presence grounds the next identification.
items.inference: The sixfold vowel root is cosmically mapped to solar rays that inwardly contain the lunar principle.
uncertainties: The exact mapping of each vowel to each ray is not specified in this verse.
items.plain_english: Those six deities are the principal rays of the sun, and within those very solar rays there is a lunar digit.

items.question: What does the lunar body signify in terms of enjoyer and enjoyable?
premises: The triad of long vowels is clearly identified as a lunar body.
The moon is not other than the enjoyable and the enjoyer.
There is no third reality apart from these two.
items.inference: The lunar principle symbolizes the nondual field in which enjoyer and enjoyable are not ultimately separate.
uncertainties: The specific three long vowels intended are assumed from the phonemic system.
items.plain_english: Therefore the triad of long vowels is clearly a lunar body; and the moon is nothing other than the enjoyable and the enjoyer—there is no third thing apart from them.

items.question: Is enjoyability an inherent property of objects like a pot?
premises: The enjoyer alone appears twofold by taking the mode of the enjoyable.
A pot does not possess enjoyability as its own independent nature.
The form of that enjoyability belongs to the subject.
items.inference: Objecthood is not intrinsic to things but is constituted in the experiencing subject.
items.plain_english: The enjoyer alone becomes established as twofold by appearing as the enjoyable; for a pot does not have enjoyability as its own nature—rather, that belongs to the subject.

rows.grounds: mode by which the unsurpassed appears

items.question: Where is enjoyability truly established and how does the unsurpassed appear as subject and object?
premises: Enjoyability is established in the subject, not in the object itself.
That establishment is what is called the object's enjoyability.
The unsurpassed appears through the modes of object-of-awareness and subject-of-awareness.
items.inference: The supreme reality manifests as both knower and known, and objecthood is grounded in that manifestation within the subject.
items.plain_english: Therefore, the establishment that occurs in the subject is called the object's enjoyability; the unsurpassed appears through the states of being the object of awareness and the subject of awareness.

rows.grounds: dynamic union of subject and object modes

items.question: How do will and the other powers become enjoyable within unsurpassed bliss?
premises: The enjoyable, such as will and the rest, attains the form of a collision.
When will and the rest are grounded in unsurpassed bliss, they become enjoyable.
This describes the dynamic interplay of the powers in the supreme state.
items.inference: In unsurpassed bliss, the powers themselves become the field of enjoyment through the collision of awareness.
uncertainties: The verse is syntactically compressed and continues into the next verse's argument.
items.plain_english: The enjoyable—will and the rest—attains the form of a collision; likewise, when will and the other powers rest on the ground of unsurpassed bliss, they become enjoyable.

items.question: How are the juncture phonemes and the blissful deity related to the enjoyer?
premises: The arising of the juncture phonemes is spoken of as the form of the enjoyer.
The god made of unsurpassed bliss is spoken of as the enjoyer alone.
Thus phonemic emergence and divine subjectivity coincide.
items.inference: The enjoyer is the blissful deity whose subjectivity is expressed in the arising of the juncture phonemes.
uncertainties: The term 'saṃdhyakṣara' may refer to specific junction vowels in the Tantric phonemic scheme.
items.plain_english: The arising of the juncture phonemes is said to be the form of the enjoyer, and the god who is made of unsurpassed bliss is said to be the enjoyer alone.

items.question: What happens to the enjoyer when the enjoyable powers dissolve into him?
premises: Will and the rest are the enjoyable and, for that reason, function as his powers.
If the enjoyable dissolves into the enjoyer, the duality collapses.
In that dissolution, the enjoyer becomes clearly manifest in reality.
items.inference: When the powers as objects are reabsorbed into the subject, the enjoyer shines forth in his true nature.
items.plain_english: Will and the rest are only the enjoyable, and for that reason they are his powers; if the enjoyable dissolves into the enjoyer, then the enjoyer becomes clearly manifest in his true reality.
